newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Cars go nowhere but statues move at Baltimore museum.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cars go nowhere but statues move at Baltimore museum.

text.p: Welcome to the museum of dreams and nightmares, of spangled cars going nowhere and sculpture that moves. It is a place for what one artist called "pieces of my life that should not have been."

The American Visionary Art Museum, perched at the edge of Baltimore's Inner Harbour, has given a home to the kinds of art often relegated to the fringe of the established art world -- items often made of found objects with homemade tools by self-taught artists. The current show is "The Wind in My Hair," which curator Susanne Theis describes as "honoring the universal desire to break free of earthly ties and touch the heavens."

-- An elaborate fan-driven mobile sculpture showing, among other things, George Washington chopping down a cherry tree, by Ben Thal, an ear-nose-and-throat surgeon in Edmonds, Washington, who carved his first work of art with a scalpel;
-- Disturbingly realistic yet surreal landscape paintings showing an owl on ice skates and a dog balancing on a hippopotamus's nose, by post-office worker Robert Sholties.

-- A barn-full of embellished vehicles including a Mercedes Benz decorated with junk jewelry by an ailing socialite, a 1951 Chevrolet truck covered with adobe and paint that functioned as a movable shrine and home, and the "Colt Mobile," a 1966 Buick studded with more than 1,000 toy horses, each symbolising a day of sobriety for its creator.

Even the museum's loading dock is scenic: tipped-over milk cans are decorated to look like pigs rooting around in trash. But, despite the off-beat feeling of the place, its founder and devoted patron, Rebecca Hoffberger, disputes those who call it a home for outcast art. "This is not 'Misfits Are Us,'" she said in an interview in a small, colourfully cluttered office just off a main gallery.

Something of a visionary herself, Hoffberger was the moving force behind the museum and the themes of the first dozen exhibitions, beginning with "Tree of Life" featuring wood constructions, through the current show, and continuing in the future to include apocalyptic art, "Lifestyles of the Down and Out" and "Soldiers' Artistic Response to War."

Much of the startup money came from her husband, LeRoy Hoffberger, from a wealthy Baltimore family, Anita Roddick, founder of the Body Shop cosmetics firm and Zanvyl Krieger, a lawyer and sports entrepreneur. But for Rebecca Hoffberger, the museum is clearly a personal crusade.

"We're not a museum in any stuffy 'mausoleum' sense," she wrote before AVAM's opening on Nov. 24, 1995, "but rather a living temple consecrated to true creative invention, intuition and fresh thought."

To that end, she engaged a pair of young architects to turn the remnants of an old paint company building and a whiskey warehouse into a four-floor museum and sculpture barn. The museum is cleaned by workers from the Baltimore Association for Retarded Citizens, not only for humanitarian reasons but because they do a good job, Hoffberger said.

A self-taught dyslexic chef runs the museum's restaurant. And instead of landscaped grounds, AVAM has a wildflower garden, not just because it seemed in keeping with the visionary theme but also for the practical reason that it needs mowing only once a year.

But it is often the artists' stories that add an uncanny dimension to the work, like C.A.A. Dellschau, a paranoid drifter born in 1830 who ended his days in 1923 confined to his daughter-in-law's home in Houston. His legacy, rescued from a trash container, includes a series of precise, gently coloured drawings, visions of a happy future that never came.
